title: Problem Overview
content: **Erdős Problem #446** studies the density δ(n) of integers having a divisor in the interval (n, 2n). This problem has two parts: (1) determine the growth rate of δ(n), and (2) determine whether δ₁(n) = o(δ(n)), where δ₁(n) counts integers with exactly one such divisor. Ford (2008) resolved both: δ(n) ≍ 1/((log n)^α (log log n)^{3/2}) where α ≈ 0.08607, and the secondary conjecture is FALSE. The problem has a 74-year history from Besicovitch (1934) through Ford (2008).
mathContext: The problem sits in analytic number theory, connecting divisor distribution with asymptotic density. The constant α = 1 - (1 + log log 2)/log 2 has a delicate definition involving iterated logarithms, reflecting deep structure in how divisors cluster near doubling intervals.

title: Divisor in Interval Predicate
content: **hasDivisorInInterval m n** holds when the integer m has at least one divisor d in the open interval (n, 2n). The definition is existential: ∃ d, n < d < 2n ∧ d | m. The set **integersWithDivisor n** collects all such m. These are the central predicates — the density of this set is precisely δ(n).
mathContext: The interval (n, 2n) is a 'doubling interval' containing n-1 integers. Divisors in this range are neither too small (trivial) nor too large (rare), making their distribution subtle.

title: Asymptotic Density δ(n)
content: **delta n** is the asymptotic density of integers with a divisor in (n, 2n), axiomatized with bounds: 0 ≤ δ(n) ≤ 1. The density is defined as the limit lim_{N→∞} |{m ≤ N : ∃d ∈ (n, 2n), d | m}| / N. This limit exists by standard analytic number theory arguments. Axiomatization is needed because formalizing the limit requires measure-theoretic infrastructure beyond Mathlib.
mathContext: Asymptotic density (or natural density) measures the 'proportion' of integers satisfying a property. It is well-defined for this set by results of Davenport and Erdős.

title: Divisor Count and δᵣ(n)
content: **divisorCount m n** computes the number of divisors of m in (n, 2n) using Finset.filter. **deltaR n r** axiomatizes the density of integers with exactly r such divisors. The **delta_decomposition** axiom captures δ(n) = Σᵣ δᵣ(n) — the total density decomposes by divisor count. This decomposition is what Erdős's secondary question probes.
mathContext: The decomposition δ(n) = Σᵣ≥1 δᵣ(n) is immediate from definitions. Erdős conjectured the r=1 term is negligible (δ₁ = o(δ)), but Ford showed each term is comparable to the total.

title: The Erdős Constant α
content: **alpha** = 1 - (1 + log log 2) / log 2 ≈ 0.08607. This constant governs the power-law decay of δ(n): the density decreases like (log n)^{-α}, which is extremely slow since α is small. The numerical bounds 0.086 < α < 0.087 are axiomatized. The appearance of nested logarithms (log log 2) reflects the fractal-like structure of divisor distribution.
mathContext: The constant α also appears in related problems about the distribution of divisors. Its small value explains why δ(n) → 0 so slowly — one needs n around 10^{10} before δ(n) drops noticeably below 1.

title: Historical Results: Besicovitch to Erdős
content: Three landmark results span 26 years: **Besicovitch (1934)** proved liminf δ(n) = 0 — the density can get arbitrarily small. **Erdős (1935)**, at age 22, strengthened this to δ(n) = o(1) — the full limit is 0, not just the liminf. **Erdős (1960)** found the correct exponent: δ(n) = (log n)^{-α + o(1)}, identifying α as the decay rate. Each result tightened the previous one.
mathContext: The progression from liminf to lim to quantitative bounds is a classic pattern in analytic number theory. Erdős's 1960 result, published in Russian (Vestnik Leningrad. Univ.), left only the secondary correction factor to be determined.

title: Ford's Exact Asymptotic (2008)
content: **ford_2008_main** gives the exact growth rate: δ(n) ≍ 1/((log n)^α (log log n)^{3/2}). The ≍ notation means there exist constants 0 < c < C such that c·f(n) ≤ δ(n) ≤ C·f(n) for all large n. The (log log n)^{3/2} factor refines Erdős's 1960 estimate. Ford's paper appeared in the Annals of Mathematics, one of the most prestigious journals in mathematics.
mathContext: Ford's proof uses sophisticated techniques from multiplicative number theory, including the anatomy of integers and sieve methods. The secondary factor (log log n)^{3/2} arises from the precise structure of smooth numbers.

title: Ford's Disproof and Generalization
content: **ford_2008_disproof** shows δ₁(n) is NOT o(δ(n)): there exists c > 0 with δ₁(n) ≥ c·δ(n) for all large n. **ford_2008_general** extends this: for each r ≥ 1, δᵣ(n) ≫ᵣ δ(n). This means no single divisor count dominates — the distribution is surprisingly flat. Erdős was 'quite sure' that δ₁ = o(δ) at Oberwolfach in 1986, but his own doubt (citing Tenenbaum's work) proved prescient.
mathContext: The disproof shows that the typical integer with a divisor in (n, 2n) has just one such divisor, contradicting the intuition that divisors should 'cluster'. The implicit constants in ≫ᵣ depend on r.

title: Primes Avoid the Interval
content: **prime_no_divisor** is a constructively proved theorem: if p > 2n is prime, then p has no divisor in (n, 2n). The proof uses Nat.Prime.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd — a prime's only divisors are 1 and itself, and neither falls in (n, 2n) when p > 2n. This illustrates that primes are 'invisible' to the density δ(n) for large enough primes.
mathContext: This is one of the few fully proved results in the formalization. It uses omega for the arithmetic contradictions after case-splitting on the prime's divisors.
